patterns.name: Single Agent
patterns.description: A single LLM-powered agent with tool access operating autonomously. All decision-making concentrated in one entity.
patterns.primaryRisk: Concentrated failure point — no redundancy, no peer validation
visualSignatures: Single box labeled 'Agent' or 'LLM' with arrows to multiple tools
One central node connected to databases, APIs, or external services
Star topology with single center and tool/service spokes

asiMappings.rationale: Single agent is the primary target for goal hijacking — no peer to detect deviation
All tool access flows through one entity — tool misuse has no checkpoint
Code execution decisions made unilaterally without review
Users interact with single agent — trust calibration has no comparative reference

patterns.name: Sequential Pipeline
patterns.description: Agents arranged in a linear chain where each agent's output becomes the next agent's input. Errors propagate forward.
patterns.primaryRisk: Cascading failure propagation — errors compound through the chain
visualSignatures: Linear chain of boxes connected by arrows flowing left-to-right or top-to-bottom
Pipeline or conveyor belt metaphor with sequential processing stages
Numbered steps (Step 1 → Step 2 → Step 3) with agent labels

asiMappings.rationale: Context passed between agents accumulates corruption — memory poisoning propagates forward
Each handoff is an inter-agent communication channel vulnerable to injection
Sequential architecture is the canonical cascading failure topology
A rogue agent mid-chain corrupts all downstream outputs

patterns.name: Supervisor-Worker
patterns.description: A supervisor agent delegates tasks to worker agents and aggregates results. Single point of control.
patterns.primaryRisk: Single point of control failure — supervisor compromise cascades to all workers
visualSignatures: Tree structure with one node at top connected to multiple nodes below
Hub-and-spoke with labeled 'Supervisor', 'Manager', or 'Orchestrator' at center/top
One-to-many delegation arrows from a controller to worker agents

asiMappings.rationale: Hijacking the supervisor redirects all worker agents simultaneously
Supervisor holds elevated privileges — identity compromise grants total access
Supervisor failure cascades to all workers — systemic single point of failure
Humans trust supervisor's aggregated output without verifying individual worker results

patterns.name: Swarm (Peer-to-Peer)
patterns.description: Multiple agents communicate as peers in a mesh network. Emergent behavior arises from collective interaction.
patterns.primaryRisk: Emergent behavior and unpredictability — collective dynamics are unauditable
visualSignatures: Mesh or fully-connected graph with bidirectional arrows between all nodes
Hexagonal or circular arrangement of agents with cross-connections
Labels like 'Swarm', 'Mesh', 'P2P', or 'Consensus' with multiple equal-sized nodes

asiMappings.rationale: Mesh communication creates maximum inter-agent attack surface
Peer propagation means one compromised agent can infect the entire swarm
Emergent behavior makes rogue detection nearly impossible — no single authority
Shared memory or context pools are vulnerable to poisoning by any peer
Swarm consensus creates false confidence — humans trust collective agreement

patterns.name: Router/Triage
patterns.description: A routing agent classifies incoming requests and dispatches them to specialized handler agents.
patterns.primaryRisk: Misclassification sends requests to wrong handler — wrong agent processes sensitive data
visualSignatures: Diamond or decision node with multiple outgoing paths to different agents
Funnel or gateway labeled 'Router', 'Classifier', or 'Triage' with branching outputs
If/else or switch-case visual metaphor with labeled branches

asiMappings.rationale: Hijacking the router redirects all traffic to attacker-controlled handlers
Router has access to all request types — privilege boundary is the classification logic
Poisoned classification context causes systematic misrouting
Misrouting creates cascading failures when wrong handler processes incompatible requests

patterns.name: Parallel Sectioning
patterns.description: Work is split into independent parallel tracks processed simultaneously, then merged. Partial failures create inconsistent outputs.
patterns.primaryRisk: Partial failure and merge conflicts — inconsistent state when some branches fail
visualSignatures: Fork-join pattern: one node splitting into parallel lanes that reconverge
Parallel horizontal lanes or swim lanes with a merge/join point
Fan-out/fan-in topology with 'Split' and 'Merge' or 'Aggregate' labels

asiMappings.rationale: Parallel execution of code across branches increases attack surface for unexpected execution
Merge point must reconcile outputs from multiple channels — injection at merge is high-value
Partial branch failure creates inconsistent merged state — cascading from merge point
Parallel tool invocations multiply misuse risk — N simultaneous tool calls

patterns.name: Reflection Loop
patterns.description: An agent iteratively evaluates and refines its own output through self-critique cycles. Risk of infinite loops and self-reinforcing errors.
patterns.primaryRisk: Infinite loop and self-reinforcing errors — no external correction signal
visualSignatures: Circular arrow or loop connecting an agent back to itself
Labels like 'Reflect', 'Self-Critique', 'Iterate', or 'Refine' with feedback arrows
Two boxes (Generator + Critic) with bidirectional arrows forming a cycle

asiMappings.rationale: Self-referential loops amplify memory corruption — poisoned context reinforces itself
Reflection without external grounding enables gradual drift toward rogue behavior
Self-reported confidence from reflection creates false assurance — automation bias amplified
Goal drift through iterative refinement — original intent erodes over cycles

patterns.name: Dynamic Orchestrator
patterns.description: An orchestrator dynamically creates, assigns, and terminates sub-agents based on runtime conditions. Unbounded delegation.
patterns.primaryRisk: Unbounded delegation and goal drift — orchestrator spawns agents without predefined limits
visualSignatures: Central node with dashed or dynamic connections to variable-count sub-nodes
Labels like 'Orchestrator', 'Planner', or 'Coordinator' with 'spawn', 'create', or 'delegate' arrows
Variable-size cluster of agents with a controller that can add/remove members

asiMappings.rationale: Dynamic orchestrator can be hijacked to spawn malicious sub-agents
Dynamically spawned agents inherit tool access without per-agent review
Privilege escalation via spawning agents with elevated permissions
Dynamic code generation for new agents enables unexpected execution
Unbounded spawning creates resource exhaustion cascades
Spawned agents may deviate from orchestrator intent — rogue by delegation

patterns.name: Group Chat/Debate
patterns.description: Multiple agents engage in structured debate or discussion to reach consensus. Vulnerable to persuasion attacks and deadlock.
patterns.primaryRisk: Consensus deadlock and persuasion attacks — one eloquent agent can dominate group decisions
visualSignatures: Multiple agents arranged around a shared space (chat room, forum, or table metaphor)
Bidirectional arrows between all participants with a shared message bus or channel
Labels like 'Debate', 'Discussion', 'Consensus', 'Vote', or 'Chat' with multiple participants

asiMappings.rationale: A persuasive agent can hijack group consensus toward attacker goals
Shared communication channel is the primary attack surface — all messages visible to all
Group consensus creates amplified automation bias — 'the group agreed' fallacy
Rogue agent in debate can systematically steer outcomes while appearing collaborative

patterns.name: Handoff Chain
patterns.description: Agents transfer full control to the next agent in sequence. Context and authority pass entirely — no shared state, no backtracking.
patterns.primaryRisk: Context loss and privilege escalation — each handoff is a trust boundary crossing
visualSignatures: Linear sequence with 'handoff', 'transfer', or 'pass' labels on arrows
Agents with clear entry/exit points and no return arrows
Baton-pass or relay metaphor with distinct agent boundaries

asiMappings.rationale: Each handoff crosses a privilege boundary — escalation via accumulated context
Context transferred at handoff can be poisoned — receiving agent trusts inherited state
Handoff channel is a high-value interception point — full context in transit
Failure at any handoff point breaks the entire chain — no recovery path

patterns.name: Human-in-the-Loop
patterns.description: Agent actions require human approval at defined checkpoints. Risk of approval fatigue leading to rubber-stamping.
patterns.primaryRisk: Approval fatigue and override bypass — humans stop reviewing after repeated approvals
visualSignatures: Agent box connected to a human icon or 'Approval' gate with yes/no paths
Checkpoint or gate symbol between agent actions with human review step
Labels like 'HITL', 'Human Review', 'Approve/Reject', or 'Manual Gate'

asiMappings.rationale: HITL is the canonical automation bias scenario — humans defer to agent recommendations
Goal hijack that produces plausible-looking outputs bypasses fatigued human reviewers
Rogue behavior masked as normal requests passes through rubber-stamp approval

patterns.name: Tool-Augmented Agent
patterns.description: An agent with access to external tools (code execution, web browsing, file system, APIs). Tool outputs become agent inputs.
patterns.primaryRisk: Tool misuse and injection via output — agent trusts tool responses without validation
visualSignatures: Agent connected to multiple tool icons (wrench, terminal, globe, database)
Function-calling or tool-use arrows with labeled tool names
Agent with 'Tools' sidebar or palette showing available capabilities

asiMappings.rationale: Tool-augmented agent is the canonical tool misuse scenario — direct tool access
Third-party tools are supply chain dependencies — compromised tool compromises agent
Code execution tool enables arbitrary code — the primary unexpected execution vector
Tool outputs can inject instructions that hijack agent goals (indirect prompt injection)
